paragraphs.context: For years I’ve wanted Jack and Annie to travel to one of my favorite cities
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why the writer chose Paris in 1889.
paragraphs.simple: The writer always wanted Jack and Annie to go to Paris. Then she found the perfect time: the Paris World's Fair of 1889. Before planes, TV and the Internet, people went to world's fairs to learn about the food, clothes and customs of other countries and to see new machines and inventions.
paragraphs.tone: Warm and friendly, like a letter to a friend.

background.note: Paris is the capital of France. It is famous for art, food, fashion and the Eiffel Tower.
The 1889 World's Fair (in French, "Exposition Universelle") was held in Paris 100 years after the French Revolution. The Eiffel Tower was built for it, and more than 30 million people came.

paragraphs.context: During the late 1800s, the world was experiencing great technological change
paragraphs.simple: In the late 1800s, machines and science changed the world very fast, even faster than today. The writer invites us to join Jack and Annie on a dangerous mission to that wonderful time.

paragraphs.context: One summer day, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the tree house story began.
paragraphs.simple: One summer a magic tree house appeared in the woods. It can take Jack and Annie to any time and place. It belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic librarian from the King Arthur stories. The tree house belongs to her.
Camelot is the castle and city of King Arthur in the old stories. Merlin and Morgan live there.

paragraphs.context: After Jack and Annie traveled on many adventures for Morgan
paragraphs.simple: Later, Merlin began to send them on "Merlin Missions". With help from Teddy and Kathleen, two young sorcerers, they went to four places from old stories and found things to help save Camelot.

background.note: Merlin is a famous wizard in the old stories about King Arthur. In the "Merlin Missions" books, Merlin sends Jack and Annie on special jobs.
Teddy is a young sorcerer and Kathleen is a "selkie" (a seal girl) from earlier Merlin Missions. Both are learning magic from Morgan.

paragraphs.context: For their next four Merlin Missions, Jack and Annie were told
paragraphs.simple: Now they must go to real places in history and show Merlin that they can use magic wisely. They have been to Venice and to Baghdad, and now they are waiting for Merlin again.

background.note: In "Carnival at Candlelight", Jack and Annie went to Venice, Italy, in the 1740s.
In "Season of the Sandstorms", Jack and Annie went to Baghdad, in Iraq, about 1,200 years ago, and helped the caliph spread wisdom.

paragraphs.context: Jack sat on the porch, reading in the summer twilight.
paragraphs.simple: It is a summer evening. Jack is reading on the porch. Crickets are singing, and an ice cream truck rings its bell down the street.

background.note: In the USA, ice cream trucks drive slowly through streets in summer, playing music or ringing a bell, and children run out to buy ice cream.

paragraphs.context: “Mom gave us money for ice cream,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go to buy ice cream.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Mom gave them money for ice cream.

paragraphs.context: “Cool,” said Jack. He pulled on his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts on his backpack and follows Annie. They can smell wet leaves and moss from the woods.

paragraphs.context: Annie stopped walking. “Listen,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie stops and tells Jack to listen.

paragraphs.context: Jack listened. “What?” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot hear anything.

paragraphs.context: “That’s the point,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says that is the point: a minute ago the crickets were loud, and now everything is very quiet.

paragraphs.context: Jack listened again. Annie was right.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is right. The whole woods seem to be holding their breath.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe,” said Annie, grinning. “Let’s go check!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie smiles and wants to go and check.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie hurried across the street and into the dimly lit woods.
paragraphs.simple: They hurry into the dark woods to the tallest oak. The rope ladder hangs down, and the magic tree house is in the branches, in the last light of the day.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. “I guess ice cream will have to wait,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiles: the ice cream will have to wait. They climb up.

paragraphs.context: Inside the tree house, dusky light filtered through the window.
paragraphs.simple: In the dim light they see a folded paper and a thin book with a red cover on the floor.

paragraphs.context: Annie grabbed the paper. Jack picked up the book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the book is a research book from Morgan. Its title is in gold letters.

paragraphs.context: “Paris World’s Fair?” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack reads the title. Annie thinks it sounds like fun, but Jack wonders why they are going.

paragraphs.context: “This should tell us,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie opens the letter. It is Merlin's handwriting.

paragraphs.context: To Jack and Annie of Frog Creek: I have discovered
paragraphs.simple: Merlin has learned that an evil sorcerer plans to steal the secrets of four new magicians at the Paris World's Fair.

paragraphs.context: Your mission is to find the magicians, warn them
paragraphs.simple: They must find the four magicians, warn them, and learn their secrets for Merlin.

paragraphs.context: “Our mission sounds more like a fairy tale than real life,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the mission sounds like a fairy tale. Evil sorcerers and magicians belong in Camelot, not in a real place like Paris.

paragraphs.context: “But we’re going to a World’s Fair,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks a World's Fair sounds a little magical.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe,” said Jack. “But why do such powerful magicians need our help
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks why such powerful magicians need help. Why can't they beat the sorcerer themselves?

paragraphs.context: “Maybe the sorcerer’s power is stronger than theirs,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the sorcerer may be more powerful.

paragraphs.context: “So maybe we can help them with Teddy and Kathleen’s rhymes,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the magic rhymes may help.

paragraphs.context: Annie gasped. “Oh, no! We need the rhyme book!
paragraphs.simple: Annie is afraid they left the rhyme book at home.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry, I have it,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has carried the rhyme book everywhere since Baghdad, in case Merlin calls them.

paragraphs.context: Jack reached into his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes out the small book from Teddy and Kathleen.

paragraphs.context: Jack turned to the table of contents.
paragraphs.simple: They used five rhymes on the last two missions, so five are left for two missions: Spin into the Air, Make Something Disappear, Pull a Cloud from the Sky, Find a Treasure You Must Never Lose, and Turn into Ducks.

paragraphs.context: “Quack! Quack!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie pretends to be a duck. She is only joking.

paragraphs.context: “You’d better not make jokes about these rhymes,” Jack said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack warns Annie: if she jokes, she might say the wrong rhyme at the wrong time and get them in trouble.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath and picked up the guide book
paragraphs.simple: Jack points to the guide book and wishes to go there.

paragraphs.context: The wind started to blow.
paragraphs.simple: The wind begins to blow.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: Then everything stops moving. It is completely quiet.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. The scent of roses floated
paragraphs.simple: The air smells of roses. Jack wears an old-style cap, a red-brown jacket and short pants. His backpack is now a leather bag.

paragraphs.context: Annie was wearing a puffy white blouse and a long purple skirt
paragraphs.simple: Annie wears a white blouse and a long purple skirt. She sees the Eiffel Tower.

background.note: The Eiffel Tower is an iron tower in Paris, 324 meters tall today. It was built in 1887-1889 for the World's Fair and was the tallest building in the world until 1930.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked. They had landed in a park filled with trees.
paragraphs.simple: They are in a park. Beyond it is a tall tower with lights at the top.

paragraphs.context: “That’s the Eiffel Tower, all right,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The fair is under the tower.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds a map in the guide book. The fair is right below the tower, so it will be easy to find.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, we need to go over what we have to do on our mission,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to talk about the mission first.

paragraphs.context: “It’s simple,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: They must find the four magicians, warn them about the sorcerer and learn their secrets.

paragraphs.context: “That doesn’t sound simple to me,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks it is a huge responsibility.

paragraphs.context: “So we’d better start now,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they should start now and leads the way down the ladder.

paragraphs.context: Jack put their World’s Fair guide into his satchel
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the guide, the letter and the rhyme book in his bag.

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie started across the park, a clinking sound
paragraphs.simple: Annie's ice cream money has changed into French coins. They may need them at the fair.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie followed a gravel path that led out of the park
paragraphs.simple: They walk to an avenue with gas streetlamps. Horse carriages and old-style bicycles go over the stones toward a bridge over a wide river.

background.note: In 1889 most streets in Paris were lit by gas lamps. Electric street lights came a little later.

paragraphs.context: Boats were gliding down the river
paragraphs.simple: Boats with lights move on the river. Thousands of little lamps shine along the river, and the Eiffel Tower glows.

background.note: The river in Paris is the Seine. The fair was on both sides of it, next to the Eiffel Tower.

paragraphs.context: “Paris is so beautiful,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie loves Paris.

paragraphs.context: “No kidding,” said Jack. “Let’s cross that bridge to the fair.”
paragraphs.simple: They join the crowd crossing the bridge.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie blended in easily with the happy crowd.
paragraphs.simple: They look like the other people. Men wear black top hats and black suits. Women wear very big hats and long, colorful dresses that puff out at the back.

paragraphs.context: There seemed to be visitors from many countries.
paragraphs.simple: There are Chinese straw hats, Dutch caps, Indian turbans and a Mexican sombrero.

paragraphs.context: “This reminds me of the carnival we went to in Venice,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers the carnival in Venice.

paragraphs.context: “Me too,” said Jack. “Except in Venice, people were wearing costumes.
paragraphs.simple: In Venice people wore costumes. Here they wear their real clothes, because it is a world's fair.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around. How would they recognize the four new magicians?
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders how they will know the magicians. Will they dress like Parisians, like people from other lands, or like Merlin in long robes? And what about the sorcerer?

paragraphs.context: “Looks like we buy our tickets over there,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees where to buy tickets.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie headed for a ticket booth near an entrance gate.
paragraphs.simple: A big banner over the gate welcomes people to the fair.

paragraphs.context: As they stood in line waiting to buy tickets
paragraphs.simple: While they wait in line, Jack reads the guide book.

paragraphs.context: Welcome to the World’s Fair—a living encyclopedia
paragraphs.simple: The fair has more than 60,000 exhibits from all over the world.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe some of the exhibits are magic shows,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks they may find the magicians at magic shows.

paragraphs.context: This World’s Fair is a showcase of progress!
paragraphs.simple: The fair shows progress: science, technology and new machines and inventions.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. “Hmm,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees nothing about magic. The fair is about inventions and science.

paragraphs.context: “How many?” the ticket seller asked gruffly.
paragraphs.simple: The ticket seller asks how many.

paragraphs.context: The ticket seller took two coins.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pays, and they walk into the 1889 Paris World's Fair.

paragraphs.context: Inside the crowded fairgrounds, below the looming Eiffel Tower
paragraphs.simple: Under the tall Eiffel Tower, a band plays, fountains shoot colored water into the sky, and a small train goes through the crowd.

paragraphs.context: People of all ages from many different countries bustled about
paragraphs.simple: People from many countries walk around, read guide books, look at exhibits and buy snacks and souvenirs.

paragraphs.context: “We can’t see much from here,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie cannot see much. It is hard to know what is happening.

paragraphs.context: “What about that little train?” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks they can ride the little train to see everything.

paragraphs.context: “Over there,” said Jack. He pointed to a clear space
paragraphs.simple: Jack points to where people get on and off the train.

paragraphs.context: They raced to the train and jumped on.
paragraphs.simple: They jump on the train. Annie pays the conductor, and they sit on a wooden bench.

paragraphs.context: “Look for anything about magic or magicians,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie to look for anything about magic.

paragraphs.context: As the train slowly chugged through the World’s Fair
paragraphs.simple: A tour guide speaks through a megaphone. The train will show the history of buildings people have made.

paragraphs.context: The train chugged by cave dwellings, canvas tents
paragraphs.simple: They pass caves, tents and mud huts.

paragraphs.context: Magic? Magicians? Jack thought as he looked
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees no magic in these buildings.

paragraphs.context: The train passed a thatched cottage, a mansion with columns
paragraphs.simple: They pass a cottage with a grass roof, a big house with columns and a palace with a golden dome.

paragraphs.context: “Now we will visit the many lands of the world,”
paragraphs.simple: Now they will see many countries. First is Egypt.

background.note: Egypt is a country in North Africa, famous for the pyramids and the Nile River.

paragraphs.context: The train chugged past an outdoor café.
paragraphs.simple: They pass an outdoor café with smells of grilled meat and coffee. Three women with veils dance to flute music.

background.note: A café is a small restaurant where people drink coffee and eat light food. Paris is famous for its outdoor cafés.

paragraphs.context: “Next we have an African village on the beautiful Serengeti Plain,”
paragraphs.simple: They pass huts in tall grass. People play drums and shake rattles. Still no magicians.

background.note: The Serengeti is a huge grassland in Tanzania and Kenya, in East Africa, famous for lions, zebras and other wild animals.

paragraphs.context: “And now we visit a New Year’s festival in faraway China,”
paragraphs.simple: They pass Chinese acrobats and a big dancing red dragon.

background.note: At Chinese New Year, a team of dancers inside a long dragon costume makes it dance through the streets for good luck.

paragraphs.context: “Dragons are sort of magic, aren’t they?” said Annie
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks dragons are a little magic.

paragraphs.context: “It’s just a couple of guys in a costume,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it is just people in a costume.

paragraphs.context: “On our left is a Muslim mosque,” the tour guide said.
paragraphs.simple: They pass a mosque, a Buddhist temple and a Japanese garden.

background.note: A mosque is a building where Muslims pray.
A Buddhist temple is a place where Buddhists pray and think quietly.

paragraphs.context: The train passed by a show with dolls dressed in outfits
paragraphs.simple: They pass dolls in clothes from around the world and a giant statue of Venus made of chocolate.

background.note: Venus was the Roman goddess of love and beauty. A chocolate company made a huge chocolate statue of her for the fair.

paragraphs.context: “It is, but it’s not magic,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack agrees it is amazing, but it is not magic.

paragraphs.context: The train rode by a globe of the world
paragraphs.simple: They pass a turning globe three stories high.

paragraphs.context: “This fair really is a living encyclopedia!” Annie said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the fair really is like a living encyclopedia.

paragraphs.context: “But the encyclopedia doesn’t have what we need to find,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it does not have what they need. He looks through the guide book.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. “Did someone just say magical?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears someone say "magical".

paragraphs.context: “False alarm,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says people are talking about the Eiffel Tower, not magic.

paragraphs.context: The train came to a stop. All the passengers were gazing up.
paragraphs.simple: The train stops. Pink lights shine on the big arches at the bottom of the tower.

paragraphs.context: “The Eiffel Tower was built especially for this World’s Fair,”
paragraphs.simple: The guide says the tower was built for this fair. It is almost 1,000 feet high, the tallest building in the world.

background.note: One thousand feet is about 300 meters. The Eiffel Tower was 300 meters tall in 1889.

paragraphs.context: People began climbing off the train.
paragraphs.simple: The train is not much help, so they get off here.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie jumped off the train just before its whistle blew
paragraphs.simple: They jump off just before the train leaves.

paragraphs.context: Iron rods rose in crisscross patterns high into the sky.
paragraphs.simple: The iron rods cross each other high into the sky. Elevators go up inside, and lights from the top sweep over the city.

background.note: The tower was designed by the company of Gustave Eiffel, a French engineer. It is made of about 18,000 iron pieces.

paragraphs.context: “It would be fun to ride to the top in one of those elevators,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to ride an elevator to the top.

paragraphs.context: “I know, but we don’t have time,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they have no time. They must find the magicians first.

paragraphs.context: “I wonder if he’s here yet,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wonders if the sorcerer is already here.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie looked around at all the people busily moving
paragraphs.simple: Everyone at the fair looks happy and excited.

paragraphs.context: No one looks like an evil sorcerer, thought Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot see a sorcerer or any magician.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s thoughts were interrupted by a young girl’s voice
paragraphs.simple: A little girl says, "It is magic!"

paragraphs.context: “Over there,” said Annie. She pointed to a nearby exhibit.
paragraphs.simple: A girl laughs while her father holds earpieces to his ears.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie walked closer to the exhibit.
paragraphs.simple: The father tells Mimi it is unbelievable.

paragraphs.context: “It’s magic, isn’t it, Papa?” said the girl.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A voice a thousand miles away.
paragraphs.simple: The girl says it can send a voice a thousand miles.

paragraphs.context: Annie grabbed Jack’s arm. “Did you hear what she just said?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie realizes this is what the Magician of Sound does.

paragraphs.context: “Right!” said Jack. He and Annie looked at the sign above the exhibit.
paragraphs.simple: They look at the sign over the exhibit.

paragraphs.context: “She’s talking about a telephone!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: It is a telephone. It is a new invention.

background.note: Alexander Graham Bell got the first telephone patent in 1876. By 1889 there were telephones in many cities, but most people had never used one.

paragraphs.context: “So Alexander Graham Bell must be the Magician of Sound!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie realizes Bell must be the Magician of Sound.

background.note: Alexander Graham Bell (1847-1922) was born in Scotland and lived in America and Canada. He taught deaf people and invented the telephone.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man, do you think Alexander Graham Bell is here in person?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders if Bell is really at the fair.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll ask,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks a woman where to find Bell.

paragraphs.context: “I do not know,” said the woman. “A strange man gave me an invitation
paragraphs.simple: A strange man gave the woman an invitation for Mr. Bell. Bell read it and left at once.

paragraphs.context: “Alexander Graham Bell!” Jack said to Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says Bell is a famous inventor, not a magician.

paragraphs.context: “The evil sorcerer must’ve heard about the telephone
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the sorcerer believes the telephone is magic.

paragraphs.context: “I wonder what that invitation said,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders what the invitation said and why the messenger was strange.

paragraphs.context: Annie tapped the gray-haired woman on the arm.

sentences.grammar: "Drew nearer" means came closer. "Like a falling feather" is a simile: it compares two things.

sentences.context: Then it fell gently onto its side, dumping Jack and Annie onto the soft, wet grass.
sentences.simple: Then the bike fell softly on its side and dropped Jack and Annie onto the soft, wet grass.

parts.text: Then it fell gently onto its side,
parts.meaning: Then the bike fell softly on its side,

parts.text: dumping Jack and Annie onto the soft, wet grass.
parts.meaning: and dropped them onto the soft, wet grass.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" phrase shows what happened because the bike fell.

sentences.context: By the time Jack had counted the 360 steps to the tower’s first-story platform, they were both panting.
sentences.simple: When Jack had counted 360 steps up to the first level of the tower, they were both breathing hard and fast.

parts.text: By the time Jack had counted the 360 steps
parts.meaning: When Jack had counted 360 steps

parts.text: to the tower’s first-story platform,
parts.meaning: up to the first level of the tower,

parts.text: they were both panting.
parts.meaning: they were both breathing very hard.

sentences.grammar: "By the time ... had counted" uses the past perfect: the counting was finished first.

sentences.context: His leg muscles burned, but he moved like a machine up the mountain of steps.
sentences.simple: His legs hurt a lot, but he kept going up the huge number of steps without stopping, like a machine.

parts.text: His leg muscles burned,
parts.meaning: His legs hurt a lot,

parts.text: but he moved like a machine
parts.meaning: but he kept going like a machine

parts.text: up the mountain of steps.
parts.meaning: up the very many steps.

sentences.grammar: "Burned" here means hurt badly. "A mountain of steps" means a huge number of steps (not a real mountain).

sentences.context: Damp with sweat, Jack felt chilled by the wind.
sentences.simple: Jack was a little wet from sweating, so the wind made him feel cold.

parts.text: Damp with sweat,
parts.meaning: A little wet from sweat,

parts.text: Jack felt chilled by the wind.
parts.meaning: Jack felt cold because of the wind.

sentences.grammar: The first phrase describes Jack and explains why he felt cold. "Chilled by" means made cold by.

sentences.context: Behind him stood an elderly man with a graying beard, a big man with a bushy white beard, and a friendly-looking man with no beard.
sentences.simple: Three men stood behind him: an old man with a beard turning gray, a big man with a thick white beard, and a friendly man with no beard.

parts.text: Behind him stood
parts.meaning: Behind him were standing

parts.text: an elderly man with a graying beard,
parts.meaning: an old man with a beard turning gray,

parts.text: a big man with a bushy white beard,
parts.meaning: a big man with a thick white beard,

parts.text: and a friendly-looking man with no beard.
parts.meaning: and a friendly man with no beard.

sentences.grammar: The place comes first and the verb "stood" comes before the people. This order is used in stories to describe a scene.

sentences.context: Since these materials are lighter than stone or brick, structures can be built very tall.
sentences.simple: Because iron and glass weigh less than stone or brick, buildings can be made very tall.
sentences.main: Structures can be built very tall.

parts.text: Since these materials are lighter than stone or brick,
parts.meaning: Because these weigh less than stone or brick,

parts.text: structures can be built very tall.
parts.meaning: buildings can be made very tall.

sentences.grammar: "Since" here means "because". "Can be built" is passive: people build them.

sentences.context: Mr. Eiffel, Mr. Bell, Mr. Edison, and Dr. Pasteur were all as still as stone.
sentences.simple: All four men were not moving at all, like stone.
sentences.main: They were as still as stone.

parts.text: Mr. Eiffel, Mr. Bell, Mr. Edison, and Dr. Pasteur
parts.meaning: All four men

parts.text: were all as still as stone.
parts.meaning: were not moving at all, like stone.

sentences.grammar: "As + adjective + as" compares two things: they were as still as stone is.

sentences.context: Jack and Annie and the others watched the giant spotlights sweep over Paris like white comets.
sentences.simple: Jack, Annie and the men watched the huge lights move across Paris like white comets.

parts.text: Jack and Annie and the others watched
parts.meaning: Jack, Annie and the men watched

parts.text: the giant spotlights sweep over Paris
parts.meaning: the huge lights move across Paris

parts.text: like white comets.
parts.meaning: like white comets in the sky.

sentences.grammar: "Watch + something + verb" (watched the spotlights sweep) means see the whole action.

sentences.context: All the motion and noise of the World’s Fair had ended for the day.
sentences.simple: All the moving and the noise of the fair had stopped until the next day.

parts.text: All the motion and noise of the World’s Fair
parts.meaning: All the movement and noise of the fair

parts.text: had ended for the day.
parts.meaning: had stopped for today.

sentences.grammar: "Had ended" is the past perfect: it ended before Jack looked around.

sentences.context: The Eiffel Tower seemed to stand watch over Paris, its spotlights sweeping over the city.
sentences.simple: The Eiffel Tower looked like a guard watching over Paris, and its lights moved across the city.
sentences.main: The tower seemed to stand watch.

parts.text: The Eiffel Tower seemed to stand watch over Paris,
parts.meaning: The tower looked like it was guarding Paris,

parts.text: its spotlights sweeping over the city.
parts.meaning: with its lights moving over the city.

sentences.grammar: "Stand watch" means stay and look out to keep people safe, like a guard. The last part (noun + -ing) adds a picture.

sentences.context: The silence of his deafness only helped him concentrate.
sentences.simple: Because he could not hear well, it was quiet for him, and that helped him think hard.

parts.text: The silence of his deafness
parts.meaning: The quiet of not hearing

parts.text: only helped him concentrate.
parts.meaning: just helped him think hard.

sentences.grammar: "Help + someone + verb" (helped him concentrate) means made it easier for him to do it.

sentences.context: But Eiffel had designed his tower so that the wind could blow safely through its open latticework.
sentences.simple: But Eiffel made his tower so the wind could go through the open crossed iron pieces without danger.

parts.text: But Eiffel had designed his tower
parts.meaning: But Eiffel had planned his tower

parts.text: so that the wind could blow safely
parts.meaning: so the wind could pass without danger

parts.text: through its open latticework.
parts.meaning: through its open pattern of crossed iron.

sentences.grammar: "So that + could" shows the purpose: why he designed it that way.

sentences.context: At first, many people thought the design was terribly ugly; others were sure the tower would topple over in strong winds.
sentences.simple: At the start, many people thought the tower looked very ugly, and others felt sure strong winds would make it fall down.
sentences.main: People thought the design was ugly.

parts.text: At first,
parts.meaning: At the start,

parts.text: many people thought the design was terribly ugly;
parts.meaning: many people thought it looked very ugly;

parts.text: others were sure the tower would topple over in strong winds.
parts.meaning: other people were sure strong winds would knock it over.

sentences.grammar: The semicolon (;) joins two related ideas. "Topple over" means fall over.

a chill down your spine.meaning: A sudden cold feeling in your back because you are afraid.
forms: a chill go down his spine
a chill down your spine.example: Jack felt a chill go down his spine.
a chill down your spine.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

a mind of its own.meaning: If a thing "has a mind of its own", it seems to move or act by itself, not as you want.
a mind of its own.example: But the bike seemed to have a mind of its own.
a mind of its own.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

all right.meaning: "It's the Eiffel Tower, all right" means it really is the Eiffel Tower. ("All right" can also mean OK.)
all right.example: “That’s the Eiffel Tower, all right,” said Jack.
all right.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as a matter of fact.meaning: In fact; really. You say it when you add a surprising fact.
as a matter of fact.example: “No, as a matter of fact, Mr. Edison was here at this exhibit just a short while ago,”
as a matter of fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at once.example: When Mr. Bell read it, he left at once.
at once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

be on your way.meaning: To leave and go. "I must be on my way" means I must go now.
be on your way.example: “Yes, I must be on my way,” said Merlin.
be on your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

blend in.meaning: To look the same as the people or things around you, so no one notices you.
blend in.example: Jack and Annie blended in easily with the happy crowd.
blend in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break into a run.example: She broke into a run and dashed toward the Hall of Machines.
break into a run.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bright and early.example: Come back bright and early tomorrow
bright and early.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bring alive.meaning: To make something seem real and exciting.
bring alive.example: bringing alive the world of engineers and inventors.
bring alive.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up to.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up to.example: He caught up to her outside the huge building made of glass.
catch up to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

clear your throat.meaning: To cough a little before you speak.
clear your throat.example: The man cleared his throat and spoke in his low, gruff voice.
clear your throat.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come back to life.meaning: To start moving or living again.
come back to life.example: the new magicians came back to life.
come back to life.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come to rest.meaning: To stop moving and stay in one place.
come to rest.example: had come to rest on the tree house.
come to rest.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

dead end.meaning: A street that is closed at one end; or a situation where you cannot go on.
dead end.example: “We’ve come to a complete dead end.”
dead end.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

draw close.example: they drew closer and closer to the tower.
draw close.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

early on.meaning: At an early time; near the start.
early on.example: Early on, a blow to his ear
early on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

end up.meaning: To be in a place or situation at the end, often without planning it.
end up.example: You might end up saying the wrong one at the wrong time
end up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fairy tale.meaning: A story for children with magic, fairies, witches or kings.
fairy tale.example: “Our mission sounds more like a fairy tale than real life,”
fairy tale.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

fall silent.example: The night fell silent as the piano music stopped.
fall silent.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

false alarm.meaning: A warning or worry that turns out to be wrong.
false alarm.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

figure out.meaning: To find the answer by thinking.
figure out.example: Then we can figure out which rhyme.
figure out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: “And find out their secrets before he does!”
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for a change.meaning: To do something different from usual.
for a change.example: we’ll try to surprise them for a change!
for a change.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for that matter.meaning: Also; and this is true for ... too.
for that matter.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get a good look.meaning: To see something well and clearly.
get a good look.example: Maybe we could ride on it and get a good look at everything.
get a good look.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get going.example: “Yikes, we’d better get going!” said Annie.
get going.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get someone in trouble.meaning: To cause problems for someone, so they are in a bad situation.
get someone in trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get the hang of.meaning: To learn how to do something.
get the hang of.example: “Go easy till we get the hang of it,” said Jack.
get the hang of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get this.meaning: "Get this!" means listen to this surprising thing.
get this.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go easy.meaning: To do something slowly and carefully.
go easy.example: “Go easy till we get the hang of it,”
go easy.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go on.meaning: To happen. "What's going on?" means what is happening? "Go on a mission" = go away to do a mission ("First they went on a mission to the city of Venice").
go on.example: It’s hard to know what’s going on.
go on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go over.meaning: To look at or talk about something carefully, to check it.
go over.example: we need to go over what we have to do on our mission,
go over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

had better.meaning: Should. "We'd better go" means we should go now.
had better.example: “So we’d better start now,” said Annie.
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hard of hearing.example: as if he were a little hard of hearing.
hard of hearing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have no idea.example: but he had no idea how to get there.
have no idea.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

have nothing to do with.meaning: To not be connected with something.
have nothing to do with.example: You have nothing to do with the invitations these gentlemen received, do you?
have nothing to do with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold on.meaning: To hold something firmly. "Hold on tight!" means hold it very firmly.
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment. "The woods seemed to be holding its breath" means everything was very still and quiet, as if waiting.
hold your breath.example: All the Frog Creek woods seemed to be holding its breath.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in disguise.meaning: Dressed or changed so that people do not know who you are.
in disguise.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in person.meaning: Really there yourself, not in a picture or on a phone.
in person.example: do you think Alexander Graham Bell is here in person?
in person.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the face of.meaning: When you have (a problem or danger) in front of you.
in the face of.example: have given many people hope in the face of disappointment:
in the face of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the first place.meaning: At the beginning; before anything else.
in the first place.example: But why do such powerful magicians need our help in the first place?
in the first place.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the near future.example: I will send for you both again in the very near future.
in the near future.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in time.meaning: 1. After some time; slowly, as time passes. 2. "In time to the music" = with the same beat as the music.
in time.example: In time it became the most beloved symbol of Paris.
in time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in your head.example: As Jack repeated his line in his head,
in your head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

just in case.example: just in case Merlin sends for us.
just in case.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

just miss someone.meaning: To arrive a very short time after someone has left.
just miss someone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep going.example: “We have … to keep going,” said Annie.
keep going.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

lead the way.meaning: To go first so other people can follow.
lead the way.example: Annie led the way down the tree house ladder.
lead the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make a joke.example: “You’d better not make jokes about these rhymes,”
make a joke.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make your way.meaning: To go somewhere, often slowly or with difficulty.
make your way.example: Annie and Jack made their way through the crowd
make your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no sign of.meaning: "There was no sign of ..." means you could not see it anywhere.
no sign of.example: There was no sign of another one.
no sign of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no use.meaning: "It's no use" means it will not help.
no use.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, brother.meaning: What you say when you feel a little tired of something or a little annoyed. It is not about a real brother.

oh, dear.meaning: What you say when you are worried, sorry or a little upset about something. It does not mean "loved" here.
oh, dear.example: “An emergency! Oh, dear!” exclaimed the woman in a high, squeaky voice.
oh, dear.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, man.meaning: What you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. It is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a man.

oh, my.meaning: What you say when you are surprised or shocked, like "Oh!" or "Wow!" Here "my" does not mean "belonging to me".
oh, my.example: “Oh, my! That’s a very long climb for two children!”
oh, my.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

on display.meaning: Being shown for people to look at.
on display.example: Many of Thomas Edison’s inventions were on display.
on display.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out loud.meaning: In a voice that other people can hear.
out loud.example: Don’t say it out loud until we need it!
out loud.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

out of breath.meaning: Breathing very fast because you ran or climbed a lot.
out of breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pay attention.meaning: To watch, listen or think carefully.
pay attention.example: I wasn’t paying attention during the carriage ride.
pay attention.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pick up.meaning: 1. To lift something up or take it in your hand ("Jack picked up the book"). 2. To start again; to go on with something. "Picked up the count" means went on counting.
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

remind someone of.meaning: To make someone think of something similar.
remind someone of.example: “This reminds me of the carnival we went to in Venice,”
remind someone of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

run into.example: What if we run into him at the institute?
run into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

send for.example: just in case Merlin sends for us.
send for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

set out.meaning: To start a trip, often with a plan.
set out.example: Join Jack and Annie as they set out on a dangerous mission
set out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

show up.example: “And the evil sorcerer hasn’t shown up yet,”
show up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

shut down.meaning: (Of a machine) to stop working, often for the night.
shut down.example: the elevators are all shut down for the night.
shut down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

spare time.meaning: Free time, when you are not working.
spare time.example: In his spare time, Edison worked on inventions.
spare time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

stand in line.meaning: To wait in a line of people.
stand in line.example: As they stood in line waiting to buy tickets,
stand in line.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

stand watch.meaning: To stay awake and guard a place.
stand watch.example: The Eiffel Tower seemed to stand watch over Paris,
stand watch.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stick around.meaning: To stay in a place and wait.
stick around.example: We stuck around until another door opened.
stick around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm.
take a deep breath.example: Jack took a deep breath and picked up the guide book
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

thanks to.example: “Thanks to Mr. Eiffel and his tower, we can see the entire city,”
thanks to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

the more the merrier.meaning: More people make it more fun, so everyone is welcome.
the more the merrier.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the size of.example: The Hall of Machines was the size of a football stadium.
the size of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

to be exact.meaning: You say this before you give the exact number or fact.
to be exact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

top hat.meaning: A tall black hat with a flat top, worn by men long ago.
top hat.example: Most of the men wore black top hats
top hat.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

topple over.example: others were sure the tower would topple over in strong winds.
topple over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn out.meaning: To happen in the end in a way you did not expect. "Turned out to be" means were, as people learned later.
turn out.example: These turned out to be the first words ever heard over a telephone.
turn out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

wait a minute.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

when one door closes.meaning: "When one door closes, another door opens": when you lose one chance, another chance comes, so never lose hope.
when one door closes.example: “When one door closes, another door opens.”
when one door closes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wipe out.example: to wipe out the bad ones!
wipe out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

word for word.example: they could hear Henri repeating his speech word for word:
word for word.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

world's fair.meaning: A very big show where many countries show their new machines, inventions, art and food.
world's fair.example: “But we’re going to a World’s Fair,” said Annie.
world's fair.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

your turn.meaning: "It's our turn" means now it is time for us (to go, to play and so on).
your turn.example: “Come on, it’s our turn,” said Jack.
your turn.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
